The ValueError comes from the for-loop: sys.argv includes the script name as element 0 ('three_sort.py'), and float('three_sort.py') raises ValueError. You must skip argv[0] and use argv[1:] for the actual numbers. Separately, min(nums).index and max(nums).index are bound methods (never called, no argument), so idxLow/idxHigh are method objects, not integers - comparing an int to a method is always unequal, so that logic can't work anyway. You don't need indices at all: once you have the three ints, low=min, high=max, and mid = sum - low - high (valid with only min/max/arithmetic). Example:

nums = [int(x) for x in sys.argv[1:]]
a, b, c = nums
low, high = min(nums), max(nums)
mid = a + b + c - low - high
stdio.writeln(str(low) + ' ' + str(mid) + ' ' + str(high))

This avoids sorting, indices, and the argv[0] pitfall entirely.

This SyntaxError is from Python's parser, not pandas. In quotechar=''') and quotechar='''') , three or four consecutive apostrophes get parsed as the start of a triple-quoted string ('''...), which is never closed - Python keeps waiting for the closing ''' and reports 'incomplete input' (and can swallow following lines/cells too, which is likely why even your third, valid attempt appeared to fail if run after a broken one in the same cell). Your third form, quotechar with a double-quoted string containing one single quote, is the correct syntax - run it on its own:

df = pd.read_csv(path, sep=',', quotechar="'")

Given your sample has a space after each comma before the opening quote, also add skipinitialspace=True so pandas recognizes the quote character immediately:

df = pd.read_csv(path, sep=',', quotechar="'", skipinitialspace=True)

That should keep 'valuec,d' as one field.

A 502 from EB usually means the upstream (gunicorn) worker died or dropped the connection, not necessarily a proxy timeout - since add_task returns the HTTP response immediately, before running generate_pdf_task, so this specific request shouldn't be blocked for 30s. Two likely causes beyond nginx/gunicorn config: (1) EB's Load Balancer (ALB/CLB) has its own idle timeout, separate from nginx and your Procfile, configurable under Configuration -> Load Balancer -> Idle timeout (default 60s) - raise that too; (2) the background task itself (PDF/zip generation) spikes memory or throws an unhandled exception on the smaller EB instance, crashing the worker process; with few gunicorn workers, the next request routed to that dead worker gets a 502. Check `eb logs` / /var/log/web.stdout.log around the failure time for OOM-killer messages or tracebacks. Consider wrapping the task body in try/except with logging, increasing instance size or worker count, or offloading PDF generation to a queue (SQS/Celery) instead of an in-process BackgroundTask.

Two frozen-app-specific issues are most likely. First, a race condition: self.browser.LoadURL() fires immediately when the frame is created, but the bundled Flask server may not be listening yet (startup is slightly slower from a frozen exe), so WebView loads a connection-refused/blank page instead of your HTML - poll 127.0.0.1:5000 (or just delay ~0.5-1s) before calling LoadURL, or retry LoadURL on a timer until it succeeds. Second, if any part of your real app uses render_template with actual template/static files, PyInstaller won't bundle them automatically - add them explicitly via --add-data "templates;templates" --add-data "static;static" in the build command/spec. Also add app.run(..., use_reloader=False) - Flask's reloader spawns a subprocess that behaves badly under PyInstaller. Finally, wx.html2.WebView on Windows defaults to the legacy IE engine unless WebView2 is available/selected; if rendering (flex layout, modern CSS) looks wrong only in the exe, explicitly request the Edge backend with wx.html2.WebView.New(panel, backend=wx.html2.WebViewBackendEdge).

Use ctypes.string_at(ptr, length) - it does a fast C-level memcpy into a Python bytes object, no Python loop needed:

length_of_return_value = c.c_uint32(0)
ptr = clib.cfunc(c.byref(length_of_return_value))
raw = c.string_at(ptr, length_of_return_value.value)  # bytes, exact length
arr = np.frombuffer(raw, dtype=np.uint8)

string_at works fine on non-string/binary data since you give it an explicit length - it doesn't stop at embedded null bytes. To avoid the extra copy, cast the pointer to a ctypes array of the right length and wrap with np.ctypeslib.as_array for a zero-copy view, then .copy() it before the C memory is freed: arr = np.ctypeslib.as_array(ptr, shape=(length_of_return_value.value,)).copy(). Important: the vector's underlying buffer was allocated on the C++ side, so Python won't free it - you need a matching C++ function (e.g. cfunc_free(ptr)) to release it after you've copied the data out, or you'll leak memory on every call.

A practical approach: evaluate f on a regular voxel grid with numpy (vectorized, not nested loops), and mark a voxel filled where f is within an adaptive threshold of zero, using the local gradient magnitude so the shell stays about one voxel thick regardless of how steeply f is scaled:

def rasterize_implicit(f, xr, yr, zr, res=1):
    xs, ys, zs = (np.arange(*r, res) for r in (xr, yr, zr))
    X, Y, Z = np.meshgrid(xs, ys, zs, indexing='ij')
    F = f(X, Y, Z)
    gx, gy, gz = np.gradient(F, res)
    grad = np.sqrt(gx**2+gy**2+gz**2) + 1e-9
    mask = np.abs(F) < grad * res * 0.5
    return {tuple(p) for p in np.argwhere(mask)}

This handles any implicit f(x,y,z)=0 without special-casing each shape; ordinary z=f(x,y) and parametric forms work once converted to implicit form. For a filled solid instead of a shell, keep voxels where f<0. If you need a watertight mesh first, skimage.measure.marching_cubes on the same grid is the standard alternative, then voxelize its triangles.

For a maintainable DRF backend: one Django app per bounded context (orders, products, users, payments), not one giant app. Within each app keep models.py, serializers.py, and either views.py (APIView/generics) or viewsets.py + routers if the API is CRUD-heavy - routers auto-generate consistent URLs and cut boilerplate. Keep views/viewsets thin: put business logic in a services.py (writes/side effects) and selectors.py (reads/complex queries) layer instead of fat views or fat models, which makes logic testable independent of HTTP. Use nested serializers or separate read/write serializers when input and output shapes differ. Version the API (api/v1/...), centralize permission/authentication classes and a custom exception handler, add pagination and filtering (django-filter) by default, and generate docs with drf-spectacular. Split settings into base/dev/prod, move slow work to Celery, and write tests per app (models, serializers, views separately). This mirrors Two Scoops of Django / DRF community conventions and scales well as the number of endpoints grows.

Generalize by building each result row directly instead of inserting one fixed value at a time - start from a copy of the original list (which already has the fixed values in place) and only overwrite the movable positions from each permutation:

from itertools import permutations

def permute_with_fixed(a, fixed_indices):
    fixed = set(fixed_indices)
    mv_idx = [i for i in range(len(a)) if i not in fixed]
    mv_vals = [a[i] for i in mv_idx]
    out = []
    for perm in permutations(mv_vals):
        row = list(a)
        for i, v in zip(mv_idx, perm):
            row[i] = v
        out.append(row)
    return out

a = [5, 6, 7, 9]
print(permute_with_fixed(a, [1, 2]))  # fixes values 6 and 7 in place

This scales to any number of fixed indices - pass a list/set like [0, 2] - without repeated .insert() calls or manual bookkeeping.

Django's built-in {% regroup %} template tag is made for exactly this - group a flat, already-sorted queryset by a field and render a header row whenever the group changes, without any transit/synthetic-row model. In the view, just order by the category field: qs = CreateNewGPR.objects.filter(name_object=pk).order_by('name_category', 'name_working') In the template: {% regroup qs by name_category as category_list %} {% for group in category_list %} {% for row in group.list %} {% endfor %} {% endfor %}
{{ group.grouper }}
{{ row.name_working }} {{ row.type_izm }} {{ row.value_work }}
{% regroup %} requires the queryset (or list) to already be sorted by the grouping key - it only detects changes between consecutive items, it doesn't sort. This avoids inflating your model/row count at all.

Self-contained equality lambdas (no outer variable) are common wherever a boolean predicate is needed as a value, most often as the key/predicate argument to another function: filter(lambda x: x == 0, values), sorted(data, key=lambda d: d['status'] == 'done') (pushes matching items to one end), any(map(lambda x: x is None, row)), or all(...)-style checks written as lambdas passed into custom validators. They're also used as tiny dispatch predicates in a list of (condition, handler) pairs, e.g. rules = [(lambda x: x == 0, handle_zero), (lambda x: x < 0, handle_negative)], or as default arguments/sentinels: def f(pred=lambda x: x is None): .... The common thread: whenever a function expects to be handed a predicate rather than call one directly (filter/sort key/dispatch table/event matcher), a self-contained lambda works because the 'external' value is baked in as a literal, not looked up from enclosing scope - useful specifically because it's reusable and doesn't depend on the caller's variables.

In GIMP 3's GObject-Introspection API, the old gimpfu constant HISTOGRAM_VALUE is exposed as an enum member: use Gimp.HistogramChannel.VALUE (not a bare Gimp.HISTOGRAM_VALUE and not the PDB's hyphenated display name) as the second argument to curves_spline - e.g. Gimp.Image.curves_spline(image, drawable, Gimp.HistogramChannel.VALUE, ...) or via pdb.gimp_curves_spline(drawable, Gimp.HistogramChannel.VALUE, ...) depending on which binding you call. For the active drawable: GIMP 3 supports multiple selected layers per image, so gimp_image_get_active_drawable was replaced by a plural accessor - use image.get_selected_drawables(), which returns a list; take the first item, e.g. drawable = image.get_selected_drawables()[0]. Generally in GIMP 3's GI bindings, PDB names become dotted method calls (Gimp.<Class>.<method>) and enums live under Gimp.<EnumName>.<MEMBER>, worth checking via dir(Gimp.HistogramChannel) if other constants give the same 'not defined' error. (Your question text was cut off before problem 3, so I can't address that part specifically.)

This is FastAPI/Starlette's automatic trailing-slash redirect (redirect_slashes=True by default) interacting badly with Vercel's serverless routing. Locally, Uvicorn happily issues a 307 redirect between /users and /users/ and your client follows it. On Vercel, your vercel.json already rewrites /api/(.*) to a single serverless function, so when FastAPI then tries to 307-redirect internally, it can conflict with or get re-wrapped by that rewrite, producing the 500/404/redirect-loop you're seeing - serverless platforms often don't preserve this redirect behavior the way a persistent dev server does. The reliable fix is to stop relying on the redirect at all: set app = FastAPI(redirect_slashes=False), then register the route without a trailing slash, @user_router.get(""), and make sure both your Next.js proxy config and any client fetch calls request that exact path (no trailing slash) consistently. That way the same route definition behaves identically locally and on Vercel, since no redirect is ever triggered in either environment.

The blowup happens because merging the grouped list column back onto the original (still-duplicated) df creates a full cross-join within each group before you explode: if a group has N original rows and its list has M duplicate codes, the merge+explode produces N*M rows for that group alone - with large groups this explodes combinatorially, matching your multi-trillion-row MemoryError. Your own fix is the right approach: deduplicate (code, Name, Age) before merging, not after, so each group only contributes its unique codes instead of every row again per list entry:

d = df[['code','Name','Age']].replace('', pd.NA).drop_duplicates()
df.merge(d, how='outer', on=['Name','Age']).dropna(subset=['code_y'])

This merges each original row against only the unique codes per group (size = number of distinct codes, not number of original rows), avoiding the N*M blowup entirely. If you only need the list itself (not one exploded row per code), df.groupby(['Name','Age'])['code'].transform(lambda s: sorted(set(s)-{''})) avoids merge/explode altogether.

This warning means your database's schema doesn't yet match Django's models for those apps. Migration files (under each app's migrations/ folder) describe how to create/alter database tables; Django ships built-in apps (admin, auth, contenttypes, sessions) with their own migrations that create tables like auth_user, django_session, etc. Until you actually run them, those tables don't exist in your database, so features depending on them (login, the admin site, sessions, permissions) will error with something like 'no such table.' Fix it by running:

python manage.py migrate

This applies all pending migrations, including your own apps' if you have any. If you've changed your own models and don't yet have migration files for those changes, run python manage.py makemigrations first, then migrate. This is a routine, expected step after starting a new Django project or pulling in model changes - not something broken.

Build one Candlestick trace per symbol (only the first visible), then add updatemenus buttons that toggle trace visibility:

import plotly.graph_objects as go

symbols = df['Symbol'].unique()
fig = go.Figure()
for i, sym in enumerate(symbols):
    d = df[df['Symbol'] == sym]
    fig.add_trace(go.Candlestick(x=d['date'], open=d['open'], high=d['high'],
                                  low=d['low'], close=d['close'], name=sym,
                                  visible=(i == 0)))

buttons = [dict(label=sym, method='update',
                args=[{'visible': [j == i for j in range(len(symbols))]},
                      {'title': sym}])
           for i, sym in enumerate(symbols)]
fig.update_layout(updatemenus=[dict(active=0, buttons=buttons, x=1.1, y=1)])
fig.show()

This is the standard 'restyle visibility per trace' pattern for a dropdown-filtered chart. With many symbols this can get heavy in a single static HTML file (one trace per symbol, all embedded) - beyond a few dozen, consider filtering the dataframe and rebuilding the figure on selection instead (e.g. via ipywidgets or a small Dash callback) rather than pre-adding every symbol as a trace.

This is an internals quirk of np.vectorize, not documented behavior to rely on. Without explicit otypes, vectorize first makes a 'trial call' on one element to infer the output dtype - that lookup uses plain array indexing (arr[0]), which preserves the numpy scalar subtype (numpy.uint8). The real elementwise pass then runs through numpy.frompyfunc, which builds a generic object-dtype ufunc and iterates via the broadcasting machinery; unboxing elements from a fixed-dtype array into that object-dtype pipeline yields native Python int instead of the numpy scalar wrapper. With list or scalar input there's no dtype-typed source array to unbox from the same way, so the original np.uint8 instance passes through unchanged both times. This is implementation detail of a function whose own docs say it exists 'primarily for convenience, not for performance', and it can differ across numpy versions. If consistent scalar types matter, avoid np.vectorize - use np.frompyfunc directly with an explicit cast, or write the loop with np.nditer specifying op_dtypes.
